articles.title: The assumption about farm automation that may be wrong
articles.dek: You've likely heard this assumption: When AI-enabled and autonomous machines arrive on the farm, jobs will disappear.
paragraphs: You've likely heard this assumption: When AI-enabled and autonomous machines arrive on the farm, jobs will disappear. But researchers at the University of California, Davis, who studied 16 fruit tree operations in California and Washington for three years, found that automation still takes human knowledge. What changes is how the work gets done. The study , drawing on 165 in-depth interviews with workers and growers, was published in the journal New Technology, Work and Employment .

The study examined what researchers call the "last mile" of agricultural automation: what happens after robotic and AI-enabled tools arrive on the farm and have to work in real conditions that can change by the hour.

"Automation isn't something that just happens to a farm or happens to a labor force," said lead author M. Anne Visser, professor of community and regional development in the UC Davis Department of Human Ecology. "People have to actively make it happen."

Every orchard is different, so technology must be adapted to each one. That often requires human knowledge about the land, the fruit or even the expected weather. No matter how good these machines get, Visser said, they may not be able to match that embedded place-based knowledge.

For example, a tractor or ATV can automatically travel down orchard rows and scan trees with a digital camera that counts buds and fruit to help forecast yield. The technology mimics a farmworker physically counting buds on every sixth or seventh tree to estimate yield.

But researchers found the technology tended to overestimate yield and often required interpretation through historical knowledge of the field. One farm manager with over a decade on the farm adjusted the camera's counts down by 14% because of historical understanding of block performance and recent weather events. His estimates ended up more accurate than the cameras'.

Even with tools in place, people are still needed to interpret what the technology is seeing, adapt it to field conditions, troubleshoot problems and bridge the gap between how a tool was designed to work and how farming actually works.

Autonomous harvesters are another example. Many prototypes can't seem to match the knowledge needed to pick fruit, Visser said. Even as the technology improves, many growers and workers believe it will still take a human to integrate it into a farm's production system and work alongside it.
"Replacing a task on a farm is not the same as replacing a job," said Visser. "These tools do not simply remove jobs on farms. They often change who does what and reshape the work around technology."

Fresh-market specialty crops are harder to automate than row crops such as corn or soybeans, Visser said, because they require quality as well as yield. Orchards are multiyear investments, and growers cannot switch out these crops in a single season. Still, as workers move into other farm roles, the technology can improve efficiency, occupational health and planning for labor shortages.
Visser said focusing only on displacement of workers can obscure opportunities for policy, workforce development, worker mobility and rural job creation.

"Our hope is that our research helps advance the conversation surrounding agricultural automation in agriculture and its impact on the labor force in a way that's more useful versus what it can often do, which is divide people pretty fast," she said.
Alex Bladimir Hernandez of UC Davis coauthored the paper.

articles.title: Public health programs can 'rewire' social networks, study finds
articles.dek: An educational program intended to improve maternal and child health fundamentally altered the social fabric of the rural Honduran villages where it was implemented, a new…
paragraphs: An educational program intended to improve maternal and child health fundamentally altered the social fabric of the rural Honduran villages where it was implemented, a new Yale-led study finds. The findings, researchers say, have implications for interventions anywhere that seek to improve people's well-being by disseminating information or changing behaviors through social contagion.

A prior study involving the same program in Honduras showed that exploiting social networks can enhance the effectiveness of public health and other interventions. This new study suggests that such initiatives also rewire existing social connections within the communities that receive them.

The study, based on a randomized controlled trial involving 8,331 people in 110 remote Honduran villages, found that the educational intervention not only changed whom people engaged with for health-related advice but also affected their friend and financial networks.

"We typically think of public health interventions as simply delivering health education with the potential of improving health knowledge and behaviors, but it turns out that they also act as social institutions that may fundamentally rewire human connections," said study co-first author Laura Forastiere, associate professor of biostatistics at the Yale School of Public Health. "Our study shows that when new information is provided, the whole structure of people's relationships, especially those based on sharing information, can be altered."

The new study was published on Oct. 14 in the journal Nature . Marios Papamichalis, a postdoctoral researcher at Yale's Human Nature Lab, is the co-first author with Forastiere. The study was also co-authored by Nicholas Christakis, Sterling professor of social and natural science in Yale's Faculty of Arts and Sciences and director of the Human Nature Lab, and Edoardo M. Airoldi, a professor of statistics and data science in the Fox School of Business at Temple University.

Interventions that exploit social influence to improve people's lives are common worldwide; they include efforts to address behaviors as diverse as microfinance uptake in India, iron supplementation in India, agricultural technology adoption in Malawi and school bullying in the United States.

For the new study, the researchers implemented a 22-month educational program promoting maternal, child and neonatal health in 110 villages in an isolated part of Honduras. Before and after the intervention, the research team mapped the villages' social networks and varied the percentage of households that received the educational program in each village. They categorized the villages as having "low-dose" participation in the intervention (5% to 30% of households) or "high-dose" participation (50% to 100%). Another set of villages in which there were not any participating households in the program served as a reference group.

In the "low-dose" villages, individuals who participated in the program broke ties with villagers who did not participate and whom they had previously consulted for health advice, a dynamic that left nonparticipants with fewer connections and reduced overall network connectivity, according to the study.
Conversely, people who received the intervention in "high-dose" villages increased their number of social ties, raising the overall connectivity of the communities' social networks.

"Think of a village's social network like a soccer team's passing game," Forastiere said. "If only a few players learn a new tactical system, like in our low-dose villages, they and their teammates stop passing to each other and the team's play breaks down. But once most of the squad learns it, as in our high-dose villages, they pass to each other more, and the whole team becomes better connected."

The health-based intervention also rewired people's friendship and financial networks, as a kind of side effect. "It may be a matter of trust," Papamichalis said. "Once you gain trust in someone, even if it is only concerning health-related matters, that trust can spread to other facets of someone's life."
The study found that the changes in village social structure induced by the educational program were durable, generally persisting three years after the intervention ended.

articles.title: Disiplinang walang palo: Challenging common Filipino parenting misbeliefs
articles.dek: More frequent spanking is linked to greater anxiety and aggression in children over time, according to international research that includes Filipino families presented by…
paragraphs: More frequent spanking is linked to greater anxiety and aggression in children over time, according to international research that includes Filipino families presented by psychology professor Dr. Liane Peña Alampay of the Ateneo de Manila University. The findings challenge the familiar belief that "pamamalo" produces more disciplined children, pointing instead to the benefits of warm relationships in the home, clear expectations and nonviolent disciplining.
In her Ateneo Breakthroughs Lecture, Alampay drew from the Parenting Across Cultures (PAC) research project, the largest multicultural and longitudinal study of its kind in the world.

Over 15 years, the PAC project followed children and their parents in nine countries—some 4,500 families in China, Colombia, Italy, Jordan, Kenya, the Philippines, Sweden, Thailand and the U. S. As the Philippine site lead, Alampay examined how parenting shapes child development and how culture influences parent-child relationships.

Across the various cultures it studied, the PAC project found that more frequent physical punishment predicted greater anxiety and aggression. Cultural acceptance of the practice sometimes weakened these outcomes, but did not transform physical punishment into a beneficial practice.
"In no instance does corporal punishment have positive effects," Alampay said, underscoring the project's findings.

"In the Philippine context, corporal punishment is often synonymous with discipline. But I want to correct that; there are many types and forms of discipline. We need to discipline our children, but in ways that are not harsh or inflicting pain," she explained.

Alampay's research also challenges the assumption that warm, accepting parenting is a Western approach unsuited to Filipino families. Across the nine countries, rejection, neglect and hostility toward the child were consistently associated with later emotional and behavioral difficulties that remained from age 7 to 14.
In contrast, children were protected from aggressive or antisocial behaviors, depression and anxiety in relationships when they felt valued and accepted.

The Filipino parents represented in the research were among those reporting the strongest authoritarian attitudes, emphasizing strictness, obedience and respect for authority. Alampay distinguished this approach from authoritative parenting , which combines rules and expectations with warmth, open communication and recognition of the child's perspective.

Moreover, close family ties also emerged as a potential strength. Valuing family responsibilities—such as helping in the home, spending time with the family, supporting siblings and respecting parents—predicted later helpful behavior and, among Filipino participants, protected against the effects of negative parenting by shaping the meanings of parent behaviors. This variable may be related but not equivalent to "utang na loob." How family obligations can bring about positive as well as negative effects among the youth needs further study.

Parenting also reflects pressures outside the home: financial hardship, unsafe neighborhoods and household instability can strain parents' well-being and relationships, increasing the risk of harsh parenting.

As a way of putting research into practice, Alampay discussed Masayang Pamilya (MaPa), a Philippine adaptation of the Parenting for Lifelong Health support intervention that aims to promote positive caregiver-child relationships, prevent violence in the home and enhance caregiver and child well-being.

articles.title: Stream restoration improves biodiversity but not necessarily ecosystem functioning
articles.dek: The EU Nature Restoration Regulation adopted in 2024 establishes the restoration of ecosystem functions as an objective of stream restoration.
paragraphs: The EU Nature Restoration Regulation adopted in 2024 establishes the restoration of ecosystem functions as an objective of stream restoration. But can conventional measures that focus primarily on restoring the physical structure of rivers and streams fulfill this task?

A meta-analysis by an international research team coordinated by the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) shows that this is not necessarily the case. Although restoration measures can improve stream structure and biodiversity, important ecological processes such as nutrient uptake and organic matter decomposition do not necessarily recover.

In their study published in Global Change Biology , the researchers therefore recommend incorporating functional indicators more systematically into monitoring and assessments of restoration success and targeting restoration measures more specifically at the functions they are intended to restore.

Many rivers and streams in Europe have been extensively modified through the construction of barriers, the reinforcement of banks and streambeds, and the straightening and channeling of streams. According to the Federal Environment Agency, fewer than 10% of rivers and streams in Germany have at least good ecological status. Structural modifications and pollutant inputs reduce biodiversity and weaken the natural self-purification capacity and resilience of rivers and streams.

Restoration measures are intended to mitigate these impacts and improve the ecological status of water bodies. Typical measures include channel reconfiguration, the removal of barriers, the reconnection of floodplains, the restoration of riparian vegetation and the addition of large wood to streams. Such measures can improve the diversity and composition of aquatic communities.

An international team of river ecologists from 13 research institutions coordinated by the UFZ analyzed 66 scientific studies to assess how ecosystem functions respond to restoration and whether they recover alongside biodiversity. They analyzed data from 281 stream sites in Europe, North America, Asia and Oceania and identified 27 functional parameters, nine of which had sufficient comparable data for the meta-analysis. These included gross primary production, nutrient uptake, denitrification and decomposition of organic matter.

These parameters reflect key processes in freshwater ecosystems and indicate how environmental pressures or restoration affect ecosystem functioning. Gross primary production involves the formation of organic biomass by algae and aquatic plants using sunlight and nutrients. Denitrification involves the conversion of nitrate into gaseous nitrogen compounds by microorganisms, including nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas.

"Hydromorphological restoration can improve biological structure, but ecosystem functions do not automatically recover as a result. Our findings show that improvements in stream structure or biological recovery do not necessarily indicate that ecosystem functions have recovered," says Ulrike Haase, lead author and doctoral researcher at TU Dresden.

The researchers also found considerable variation in the effects of restoration measures on ecosystem functions. Of the nine functions studied, denitrification was the only one for which rates were significantly lower in restored than in degraded streams. "However, this does not automatically mean that the function has deteriorated. Lower denitrification rates may also indicate lower nutrient enrichment," says Dr. Mario Brauns, a UFZ river ecologist who coordinated the study and is a co-author.

For the remaining functions, no clear differences were found between restored and degraded streams. "This shows that the restoration measures commonly used to date are usually not sufficient on their own to ensure a measurable recovery of the ecosystem functions we studied," says Brauns. By contrast, biological characteristics such as species diversity, abundance and biomass generally improved following restoration. "However, we can assess whether an ecosystem function is actually recovering only if we know its status under appropriate reference conditions," concludes Brauns.

Ecosystem functions have received little attention in assessments of restoration measures despite the explicit call to restore natural river functions in the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030. The Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework also identifies the restoration of ecosystem functions as a goal. "Quantifying ecosystem functions such as gross primary production or nutrient uptake often requires considerable effort," says Brauns. Compared with biodiversity, ecosystem functions still lack widely standardized assessment procedures and suitable reference values.

articles.title: Study: Pandemic arrest patterns may have deepened existing inequalities in policing
articles.dek: The COVID-19 pandemic was a public health crisis that affected more than the public's health.
paragraphs: The COVID-19 pandemic was a public health crisis that affected more than the public's health. It brought complex changes across many aspects of society, including having an influence on suburban arrest patterns, according to a study co-authored by University at Buffalo researchers.
Using data in Irondequoit, a suburb of Rochester, New York, the research team found that the pandemic intensified existing racial disparities in policing.

"Many of the already well-documented patterns in arrests increased during the pandemic," says Christopher Dennison, Ph. D. , an associate professor of sociology and criminology in the UB College of Arts and Sciences, one of the study's co-authors. The study was led by O. Nicholas Robertson, Ph. D. , an associate professor of criminal justice at the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT), along with Robert Adelman, Ph. D. , UB professor of sociology and criminology, with several UB and RIT graduate students also co-authoring.

After any social upheaval or periods of turmoil or civil unrest, researchers often look at major cities to explore how existing patterns of behavior might have changed, but the current study was an opportunity to explore a suburb, a community type that isn't often the focus of research.

"A society can become very fragile when it experiences something that creates widespread conditions of uncertainty," says Dennison. "We see that here. And though our findings aren't generalizable, we've provided enough initial evidence to make additional studies like ours, that look at small towns rather than big cities, worthy of further consideration.
"Systemic inequalities were made worse, and that's something that deserves a closer look."
The results are forthcoming in the American Journal of Criminal Justice .

Irondequoit's population is about 50,000 people. White people comprise 73% of the population, Black people 10% and Hispanics 9%, according to 2023 census data. Using records from the local police department, the research team plotted out the arrests year by year from the two years before the pandemic (2018–19); during the pandemic (2020–21); and the two years after its most significant impacts (2022–2023).

"One of the reasons criminologists explore arrests and early system contact is because those points aren't examined as much as conviction and incarceration," explains Dennison. "But these points can have profound effects.
"We know through research that these arrests are potentially harmful and researchers are becoming increasingly more aware that harm does not begin with a conviction."

Initially, arrests declined generally during the early stages of the pandemic, relative to the prior two years. In 2021, however, there was an increase in arrests for alleged nonviolent crimes, particularly among Black individuals.

Among the study's other findings: Violent crime decreased through 2020, with no substantial increase during later study points. As for differences between men and women, both groups experienced increases in arrests following the onset of the pandemic, with men exhibiting a rate of approximately 37 arrests per 1,000 individuals by 2023, with women at almost seven arrests per 1,000 individuals.
"Further study is needed in this area," says Dennison. "It's not about planning for the next pandemic but exploring response strategies during major upheavals."
Journal information: American Journal of Criminal Justice

articles.title: Ants break a basic rule of biology to help them adapt to new environments
articles.dek: A new study led by researchers in the Eco-Evo-Devo lab at the University of Ottawa finds that ants can decouple antenna size from both head and body size as they develop into…
paragraphs: A new study led by researchers in the Eco-Evo-Devo lab at the University of Ottawa finds that ants can decouple antenna size from both head and body size as they develop into different social castes, revealing how social signals and hormones help shape traits for specialized colony roles.

Bigger animals usually have bigger body parts. It's one of biology's most familiar patterns. Yet some ants appear to break that rule. The discovery offers a new view of how evolution can loosen biological constraints and produce new combinations of traits.
The study, titled " Breaking trait scaling via the evolution and regulation of dimorphic decoupling in ants ," is published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences .

The researchers studied Pheidole, a highly diverse genus of ants whose colonies include small workers and much larger soldiers. Within each caste, antennae still grow in proportion to body size. Surprisingly, across castes, the relationship changes: the ranges of worker and soldier antenna sizes completely overlap, despite the fact that soldiers have substantially larger heads and bodies.

"It was total serendipity. We were sitting at the microscope and Erica (Erica Vong is a graduate researcher and student at uOttawa and lead author of this study) showed me the antennae of two individuals. One was clearly smaller, yet it turned out to be from the soldier," says Rajendhran Rajakumar, associate professor in the Department of Biology at uOttawa's Faculty of Science; the research was conducted in his lab.
"Much like when you are getting your favorite latte, both castes have small, medium and large sizes of overlapping antennae."
It turns out that the big antennae were from the biggest worker and the small antenna was from the smallest soldier, which is still much bigger in both head and body size.

"Biologists have long assumed that traits such as antennae generally scale predictably with body size," Rajakumar says. "Our findings show that evolution can decouple a trait from body size in one context while preserving that relationship in another."

The team combined laboratory experiments, field data, museum collections and comparative analyses. Measurements from 565 Pheidole species showed that this unusual antennal pattern is widespread across the genus. Comparisons with other ants suggest it may have originated near the common ancestor shared by Pheidole and the closely related Cephalotes turtle ants.

Antennae are essential to an ant's survival. Ants use them to detect chemical and physical cues, find their way through their surroundings and communicate with nestmates—all critical in the functioning of their societies. Their size and shape can also affect the number and arrangement of sensory structures available to each ant.

"The antenna is not simply getting bigger because the ant is bigger," Rajakumar explains. "In these colonies, development preserves a flexible range of antennal forms that may help individuals compatibly respond together to changing environmental demands."

Experiments with Pheidole dentata showed that this flexibility is regulated by the colony's social environment, juvenile hormone and signals from an allometry-regulating organ. Previously, Rajakumar had played a role in work that had demonstrated that these same factors are critical for soldier and supersoldier development.

By changing these factors, particularly the soldier inhibitory pheromone, the researchers now produced novel "nanoworkers" and "nanosoldiers"—nanosoldiers with the body size of a worker and the head size and shape of a soldier. These ants revealed body-and-trait combinations that ordinary development usually keeps hidden, yet the developmental potential exists and can be activated.

The results also show how the colony acts as a superorganism , with social conditions influencing the development of individual ants. "Social signals and hormones do more than determine whether an ant becomes a worker or a soldier," clarifies Rajakumar. "They can also reshape how different traits grow and scale together (or decouple), within castes, between castes and more broadly across species."

articles.title: Researchers Discover a Surprising Twist in How Our Cells Age
articles.dek: Scientists uncover a surprising paradox in how our cells age, revealing that more cellular cleanup isn’t always better and exercise may help restore a youthful balance.
paragraphs: Scientists uncover a surprising paradox in how our cells age, revealing that more cellular cleanup isn’t always better and exercise may help restore a youthful balance.

Every day, our cells must dispose of damaged proteins and other unwanted material to keep themselves functioning properly. They accomplish this through a natural recycling process called autophagy, which packages cellular waste into specialized compartments where it is broken down into smaller molecular components that can be reused.

By preventing harmful waste from accumulating, autophagy plays an important role in maintaining cellular health. Scientists have long believed that this cleanup system gradually becomes less effective as people grow older. Declining autophagy is widely considered a hallmark of aging and has been associated with conditions such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disorders.
However, a new study suggests that the relationship between aging and cellular recycling is far more complicated than previously assumed.

Researchers at Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute reported their findings in the journal Aging Cell . Rather than finding a consistent decline in autophagy with age, they discovered that recycling activity follows different patterns depending on the type of cell and whether it comes from a male or female participant. Their results also suggest that physical exercise may influence this process in humans.

“We commonly see people cite this idea that autophagy declines with age, but the actual evidence for this in humans is very thin,” said senior and corresponding author Caroline Kumsta, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.
“Interest is growing in targeting autophagy to develop new healthy aging interventions,” said Tatiana Moreno, PhD ’26, the study’s lead author and a former graduate student in Kumsta’s laboratory.
“We wanted to challenge assumptions and investigate what actually happens to autophagy during aging in healthy individuals.”

To investigate how autophagy behaves throughout adulthood, the scientists collected blood and skin samples from volunteers between 23 and 72 years old. All participants reported that they were free of chronic diseases. The researchers also converted some of the collected skin cells into induced neurons, allowing them to examine a third type of cell.

The team then analyzed RNA transcripts in each cell type. These transcripts are produced when genetic instructions stored in DNA are “read” as part of the process of making proteins, enzymes, and other essential cellular components. By examining the transcripts, the scientists could investigate how aging and cell type affected the activity of genes involved in autophagy.

Importantly, the researchers did not rely solely on these genetic measurements. They also directly measured how quickly cells carried out autophagy, making it possible to determine whether patterns of gene expression accurately reflected the recycling process itself.
The results challenged the conventional view that autophagy steadily weakens throughout the body as people age.

“We found that autophagic activity changes were not universal throughout the body and did not follow the idea that autophagy simply declines with age,” said Kumsta. “Rather, cellular recycling rates are altered differently with age in each of the cell types, and differently by sex in each of the cell types.”

In skin cells from male participants, autophagy activity decreased with age. However, the same process remained relatively constant in skin cells from female participants. Even more unexpectedly, induced neurons derived from female participants showed increased autophagy as age advanced.

articles.title: Scientists Discover Chronic Back Pain Can Change How Your Brain Sees You
articles.dek: A chronic back pain flare may switch on a brain network tied to identity, linking physical pain with how you see yourself.
paragraphs: A chronic back pain flare may switch on a brain network tied to identity, linking physical pain with how you see yourself.

Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered flares in people with chronic low back pain activated a brain network associated with identity and inward reflection. Painful heat produced the opposite response, suggesting that a familiar back pain flare engages the brain differently from a new external threat.

Low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide, according to the World Health Organization. For people with chronic low back pain (cLBP), which lasts longer than 12 weeks, everyday movements can bring sudden spikes in pain, adding fear and uncertainty to ordinary activities.

The findings, published October 5, 2026, in the British Journal of Anaesthesia , offer a possible explanation for why treatments focused on pain symptoms often fall short. They also raise the possibility of treating the relationship between pain and identity.

The study involved 114 people with cLBP who performed a “leg raise test,” a standard procedure used to provoke back pain. Researchers measured brain blood flow using arterial spin labeling, a specialized functional MRI technique. Participants also received a painful but harmless heat stimulus on the calf, providing a comparison with acute pain from an external source.

During movement-triggered flares, the Default Mode Network (DMN) became more active. This collection of connected regions across the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes helps support thoughts about personal identity, memories, and internal feelings. Its involvement in inward reflection has earned it the nickname “self-network.”

Painful heat, by contrast, reduced DMN activity. According to corresponding author Fadel Zeidan, this response allows attention to shift toward an outside threat, such as something hot touching the skin.

“In every pain study, when you’re experiencing pain, the DMN deactivates,” said Zeidan. “What we show for the first time ever is that when you have a pain flare, it turns on instead. You start to identify the experience with who you are.”

The brain scans also revealed differences related to pain severity. Participants with worse chronic back pain had stronger connections between the DMN and the primary somatosensory cortex, which processes bodily sensations, including those from the back. More intense pain during the leg raise test corresponded to greater activity in sensory and motor regions, while heart rate increases reliably tracked the intensity of the flare.

Together, these findings suggest that a flare may draw on more than the immediate physical experience. Memories of earlier episodes, expectations about what movement will feel like, and worries about its consequences may all become part of the experience.

“The moment-to-moment experience is contaminated not only by the feeling of pain, but by the anticipation of it and recovery from it. It’s contaminated by past experiences like embarrassment about not being able to participate in normal activities and fear of movement when trying to avoid the pain.”

The team suspects that these different patterns of brain activity help explain why conventional pain treatments, including opiates, often provide insufficient relief for movement-triggered chronic pain.
“Current pain medicine is fixated on ridding patients of their pain symptoms, but that’s not the source of chronic pain. These data suggest that a chronic pain flare also encompasses one’s identity.”

Zeidan’s team has separately investigated mindfulness meditation and the psychedelic compound psilocybin as approaches that may help people separate pain from their sense of self. Early studies have reported reductions in pain intensity, although larger studies are needed to confirm the benefits and clarify how they occur.

articles.title: Cannabis May Be Sabotaging Your Sleep Without You Even Knowing It, Study Finds
articles.dek: Nearly 35 years of observational data link greater lifetime cannabis use to poorer sleep in middle age, challenging its reputation as a sleep aid.
paragraphs: Nearly 35 years of observational data link greater lifetime cannabis use to poorer sleep in middle age, challenging its reputation as a sleep aid.

More than eight hours of sleep might sound like a good night’s rest, but a new Northwestern Medicine study linked recent cannabis use to both a greater likelihood of sleeping that long and more disrupted nights. The fragmented sleep and longer stretches awake recorded by wrist-worn monitors were not reflected in participants’ own sleep ratings, suggesting that people may not notice these disturbances.

The study, published October 9 in JAMA Network Open , analyzed data from 1,266 participants in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) Study. This community-based study began in 1985–86 and follows Black and white adults across the U. S.

Researchers repeatedly tracked participants’ cannabis use over nearly 35 years, from young adulthood into middle age. In middle age, participants wore a wrist-based sleep monitor for a week and completed sleep surveys, allowing the team to compare recorded sleep patterns with people’s impressions of their own sleep.

Millions of Americans use cannabis as a sleep aid. “This study challenges the common belief that cannabis helps people sleep better,” said corresponding author Dr. Thanh-Huyen T. Vu, research associate professor of preventive medicine (epidemiology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. “Our findings suggest cannabis may actually be associated with poorer sleep quality, even if people don’t perceive those changes.”

Greater cumulative cannabis use was associated with lower sleep efficiency, meaning participants spent a smaller percentage of the night asleep. Their sleep was also more fragmented, and they spent more time awake after initially falling asleep. Compared with people who had never used cannabis, recent users showed similar patterns and were significantly more likely to sleep longer than eight hours a night.

“This was one of the most interesting findings,” Vu said of the comparison between the monitor readings and participants’ sleep surveys. “The wearable device detected more nighttime disruption among participants with long-term cannabis exposure, but the participants themselves generally did not report worse sleep.”

The associations with poorer objectively measured sleep remained after researchers accounted for numerous factors known to affect sleep, including age, sex, race, cigarette smoking, alcohol use, physical activity, depression, chronic health conditions, and use of other substances. The study was not designed to determine whether cannabis directly causes sleep problems, so the findings establish an association rather than a causal effect.

“Our data do not support the belief that cannabis is helpful as a sleep aid,” said senior author Mercedes R. Carnethon, chair of the department of preventive medicine at Feinberg. “As cannabis becomes increasingly available and accepted, it’s important to better understand its long-term associations with health behaviors such as sleep.”

The analysis of long-term recreational cannabis use did not distinguish between consumption methods such as smoking and eating edibles. Patterns of cannabis use likely changed over the decades participants were followed, making consumption methods an especially important question for future studies, the authors said.

For people seeking better sleep, well-established strategies can improve sleep quality, said study co-author Kristen L. Knutson, associate professor of neurology (sleep medicine) and preventive medicine (epidemiology) at Feinberg.

“Keep a regular bedtime, make your bedroom cool, dark and quiet, and avoid looking at phones and other screens right before bed,” Knutson said. “It can also help to establish a calming routine before sleep, such as reading, meditating or taking a shower. If sleep problems persist, or if you’re a loud snorer, talk with your health care provider to rule out an underlying sleep disorder.”

The Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study is conducted and supported by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) in collaboration with the University of Alabama at Birmingham (grants 75N92023D00002 and 75N92023D00005), Northwestern University (grant 75N92023D00004), University of Minnesota (grant 75N92023D00006), and Kaiser Foundation Research Institute (grant 75N92023D00003). The CARDIA Sleep Ancillary Study is funded by grant R01HL152442 from the NHLBI.

articles.title: NASA’s Hubble Charts Path for Roman with Gravitational Lenses
articles.dek: A sweeping barred spiral galaxy marks the spot in this image, but the real treasure is the gravitational lens in the lower-right corner, where a distant background galaxy is…
paragraphs: A sweeping barred spiral galaxy marks the spot in this image, but the real treasure is the gravitational lens in the lower-right corner, where a distant background galaxy is being magnified and distorted by the gravity of a closer galaxy.
This observation is one of many gravitational lensing images taken by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope in preparation for science with the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope .

Gravitational lensing occurs when the mass of a foreground object – such as a galaxy – warps spacetime, causing light to bend, distort, and magnify as it passes around the object, similar to a giant lens in space. Lenses like this occur when a precise chance alignment takes place between the foreground and background galaxies, causing light from the background galaxy to curve around the foreground galaxy.

In this image, the gravitational lens features a foreground elliptical galaxy that is about 4. 5 billion light-years away. That means the light we see from this galaxy now would have first started traveling toward us when our solar system was still forming. The background galaxy is about eight billion light-years away, almost twice as far. It appears as a pair of arcs, one large and very noticeable to the upper left of the foreground galaxy, the other a much smaller, flipped image of the same background galaxy to the lower right. This configuration is called an arc-counterarc pair.

The more massive the foreground galaxy is, the stronger the gravitational lens and the more significantly it bends light. By studying the distortion of the background galaxy, researchers can determine how much mass the foreground galaxy contains. This plays a huge role in the study of dark matter, the mysterious, invisible substance that makes up the majority of mass in the universe. The visible matter is not enough to account for the level of distortion in the background galaxy, which allows researchers to calculate both the mass of the foreground galaxy and how much dark matter it contains.

Almost all of the objects in this image are galaxies, except for a few scattered foreground stars. The barred spiral galaxy in this image – so called because its arms extend from a bar of stars in its center – is about the size of our own Milky Way galaxy, which astronomers think is a barred spiral as well. The tiny spiral to the left of the large spiral may be a satellite galaxy, similar to the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds that orbit the Milky Way.

Hubble views the cosmos primarily in visible and ultraviolet light with some infrared coverage, and Roman sees mainly infrared wavelengths and some visible light. Hubble can provide high-resolution views of individual objects, while Roman has a much larger field of view conducive to panoramas.

Images like this offer a glimpse of how Hubble and Roman will work together to build an even more comprehensive picture of the cosmos. This is just one of many gravitational lens images captured by Hubble. Astronomers will use them to analyze gravitational distortions to learn more about dark matter in the foreground galaxies and to lay the groundwork for future Roman observations.

Hubble can only view these gravitational lenses one at a time, while Roman’s wide view of the sky will provide a greater sample of these lenses. Astronomers are using Hubble’s sharp images to build a computer model to better analyze dark matter-induced distortions. This tool will help astronomers analyze Roman’s large images. Hubble will also follow up on interesting lenses Roman detects.

articles.title: Surviving cancer starts at diagnosis and continues after treatment – earlier survivorship care can help patients feel better and live longer
articles.dek: “You have cancer.” It’s a phrase that comes as a shock, then is quickly followed by a whirlwind of decisions that somehow feel fast and slow at the same time.
paragraphs: “You have cancer.” It’s a phrase that comes as a shock, then is quickly followed by a whirlwind of decisions that somehow feel fast and slow at the same time.

You have treatments to decide on. You are trying to figure out how you might work, care for your family and undergo a variety of intensive medical appointments all at the same time. You are centered on the here and now, and thinking about five or 10 years down the road is not at the forefront of your mind. Getting through treatment is the finish line you are reaching for; that is when you may actually feel like a cancer survivor.

As a nurse and scientist who has spent over a decade caring for cancer patients and studying ways to ease the effects of treatment, I have heard this story time and time again from both survivors and their loved ones. But survivorship actually begins at the time of diagnosis.

In fact, in our newly published research in JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery, my team and I found that patients with head and neck cancer who started survivorship care – healthcare services that support a cancer survivor’s physical, emotional, social and practical needs – earlier were more likely to stick to treatment and be alive without cancer three years after treatment.

Clinicians and researchers consider a person a cancer survivor from the time they are diagnosed through the end of their life. More important than the term is what cancer survivorship is meant to look like for the patient.

Cancer survivorship reflects the patient’s experience with cancer and cancer treatment, and the physical, emotional and social effects that has on their life. Survivorship care is designed to identify and address the complex needs of a cancer survivor beyond just the physical changes. It involves coordinating care and promoting the person’s overall health and well-being.

This care can look different for each patient, depending on the cancer they have and their individual needs. For example, my team and I designed a survivorship clinic at UPMC in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to address the most common issues head and neck cancer survivors experience. In addition to surgeons and nurses, our team includes swallowing therapists, a physical therapist, a dental care team and a dietitian to help address issues with swallowing, nutrition, dental health, physical function and mood. All of these services are offered at the same location and can be completed in one visit on the same day, generally under one copay.

After the visit, the cancer survivor, their oncology team and their primary care clinician receive a care plan to help coordinate care and communication among all their providers. Rather than as a one-time session, our survivorship clinic builds relationships with survivors, supporting them as their needs change over time.

While a person becomes a survivor at the time of diagnosis, most survivorship care is delivered after the initial treatment has ended. This may be partly because to be accredited by a major medical body that sets cancer care standards, the American College of Surgeons Commission on Cancer , hospitals must offer at least three services to cancer survivors after they complete their initial treatment.
While survivorship care can ease physical and psychological issues after cancer treatment, survivors often report significant unmet needs before and during treatment.

In my specialty of head and neck cancers, many patients undergo a grueling five to seven weeks of radiation therapy, often in addition to chemotherapy. They experience a host of side effects: pain, mouth sores, skin burns, difficulty swallowing and weight loss, which together can lead to treatment interruption and hospitalization . These side effects often continue and sometimes worsen years after treatment .

While our survivorship clinic was initially designed for patients who completed treatment, we later expanded our services to patients before radiation. We previously found that starting survivorship care before radiation was associated with better quality of life and reduced symptoms .

In our newly published research, we found that among 471 cancer survivors, 62% of those who attended our survivorship clinic before completing radiation finished treatment on time , compared with 48% of those who were not seen before completing radiation. At three years, 60% of patients seen in the survivorship clinic before completing radiation were alive and cancer-free, compared with 39% of those not seen before completion. The association remained after accounting for whether patients completed radiation on time, suggesting that on-time completion may not fully explain the difference.

Although our results suggest that shifting the start of survivorship care to before treatment may improve outcomes, they do not prove it. Our team plans to test in a larger clinical trial whether starting survivorship care before radiation helps patients finish treatment on time and maintain quality of life, while also examining how teams coordinate care and referrals.

Comprehensive cancer care implies not only a comprehensive treatment plan, but also supportive care that will help patients live well beyond their diagnosis and treatment. However, a 2024 survey of 384 facilities accredited by the American College of Surgeons Commission on Cancer found that only 1 in 5 programs estimated that most of their eligible patients receive survivorship care .

For head and neck cancer survivors specifically, nearly all clinicians routinely assess cancer recurrence, swallowing and thyroid function. But only about half address psychological symptoms , such as anxiety and depression, and fewer than 1 in 3 addressed body image or sleep problems.

Survivorship care is often framed as care that begins after treatment ends, which can delay patients’ access to support during treatment. Communication breakdowns may leave patients unaware of available services, while a lack of referrals can keep them from receiving needed care. Survivorship care also draws on clinicians with different areas of expertise, and some hospitals and treatment centers may lack enough dedicated staff time to provide a full range of services.
The end of treatment is a huge milestone that patients and their loved ones reach for. But it is not where survivorship care truly starts.

Making survivorship care more accessible may help make cancer care more comprehensive. Clinicians and researchers can start planning for the survivor’s life after cancer even when it’s not on the patient’s mind. Bringing a team that combines treatment experts with rehabilitation and supportive care specialists into the room early can help achieve better outcomes for patients.
As a cancer survivor or a loved one, you don’t need to wait.

Marci Lee Nilsen receives funding from the National Institutes of Health and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation. She directs the UPMC Head and Neck Cancer Survivorship Clinic, which was the setting for the research described in this article.

articles.title: Archaeologists Discover Lost Roman Fort That Could Rewrite an Ancient Welsh Legend
articles.dek: Pottery, coins, and buried defenses point to a Roman fort in west Wales, offering a possible setting for Emperor Magnus Maximus’s camp in medieval Welsh folklore.
paragraphs: Pottery, coins, and buried defenses point to a Roman fort in west Wales, offering a possible setting for Emperor Magnus Maximus’s camp in medieval Welsh folklore.
My recent discovery of a Roman fort and its extraordinary connection with medieval folklore was the fruition of many hours of painstaking research.

This all began in 2002 when I discovered, or, more accurately, rediscovered, a Roman villa some 30 kilometers to the southwest of Wales . The site was first identified in the early 19th century by Richard Fenton , a local antiquarian. For several reasons, his reliability has been questioned, but mostly because of the perception that the Romans did not reach west Wales, which was rife in the Regency period and persists to this day.

When my team and I were digging the villa, a local volunteer asked what a Roman site of this status was doing in the middle of nowhere. This was a good question, and I did not know the answer. However, the archaeologist Sir Mortimer Wheeler dug a similar site on the same latitude in 1922, and I reasoned that both sites could lay close to a Roman road. This began a quest to trace a network of routes through west Wales.

A stretch of Roman road was in fact identified by Fenton in the vale of Whitland. This was excavated in 1995, in advance of the construction of a bypass, but I felt that there was more of a network to be discovered. I made a breakthrough in 2022. Several other Romano-British sites have been discovered since Wheeler’s day, including a fort at Wiston near Haverfordwest in 2012–2013, and several villas.

Like Fenton, my observations have attracted a good deal of skepticism, but my heart and mind felt that I was making considerable progress tracing the Roman road network from Pembrokeshire east into Carmarthenshire.

My theory received a boost in 2024 with the observation of earthworks suggestive of a Roman auxiliary fort adjacent to an almost certain Roman road near Crymych in north Pembrokeshire. The earthworks had a characteristic playing-card shape like auxiliary forts and was about three hectares in area, which is typical for this type of military installation.

One corner has been destroyed by the construction of a post-medieval settlement (the village of Crymych), which is still inhabited today. The south of the enclosure is intersected by a leat (aqueduct) that enters the site through a masonry channel. Every Roman fort, of course, needed a water supply. The site lies adjacent to the A478, which runs straight in that area, and many sections further south are similar, but the line is lost in places, which is often the case with Roman roads.
It is my belief that it is part of a previously unidentified major arterial Roman road connecting modern Pembrokeshire with Ceredigion to the north.

My hypothesis gained traction with the results of a limited geophysical survey in October 2025, which placed two rectilinear (straight-lined and right-angled) buildings in the right place. Trial excavations followed in March and July 2025, and a steady trickle of finds followed, including coins, a gaming counter, some Roman pottery, and a spindle whorl for spinning wool. A more comprehensive evaluation excavation was needed, however, to establish for certain whether the site was a Roman auxiliary fort.

When I discovered the site in 2024, I began to think that it may relate to Cadair Maxen, the camp of the Roman emperor Magnus Maximus (Macsen Wledig in Welsh). He’s mentioned in the Mabinogion (a collection of medieval Welsh stories) in The Tale of Emperor Maxen, also known as The Dream of Macsen Wledig .

This places the late 4th-century usurping emperor on the Frenni Fawr, the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which dominates the site a little over three kilometers to the northeast. However, there are no visible remains of a Roman marching camp on the Frenni Fawr where the emperor is said to have visited.

Our breakthrough came in early September with the excavation of five trenches. Three across the suspected principal buildings (the commander’s house, headquarters building, and granaries); one in the area to the north where a perimeter road would be expected; and another up-slope where the geophysical survey (non-invasive ground scans detecting buried stone structures and drainage ditches beneath the soil) indicated a track.

articles.title: These Mysterious Underwater Reefs Could Help Save Marine Life As Coral Reefs Decline
articles.dek: Submerged ancient forest floors off Mozambique now shelter young reef fish, suggesting overlooked peat reefs could offer some species refuge as coral reefs decline.
paragraphs: Submerged ancient forest floors off Mozambique now shelter young reef fish, suggesting overlooked peat reefs could offer some species refuge as coral reefs decline.

Much of the seabed along Mozambique’s Bazaruto coastline is shifting sand, leaving marine life few solid places to settle and shelter. Exposed layers of ancient peat provide that foothold, supporting fish communities comparable in diversity to those on a nearby coral reef.

These submerged “peat reefs” began as coastal swamps and forests. Their plant remains accumulated into peat, a compressed, carbon-rich material. As sea levels rose over the past few thousand years, the sea flooded these landscapes. Waves later stripped away the overlying sand, exposing firm platforms that marine life could colonize.

A study published in Scientific Reports documents these habitats in the shallow waters of the Bazaruto Archipelago in the Western Indian Ocean. Researchers from the Bazaruto Center for Scientific Studies (BCSS) Ocean Observatory worked with collaborators at universities and research institutions in the United Kingdom, United States, and Canada. The work is believed to be the first ecological study of tropical peat reefs and the first anywhere to examine peat reefs from a biodiversity perspective.

The team surveyed three peat reefs and a nearby coral reef, comparing seabed cover, invertebrates, small fish, and larger animals such as sharks, rays, and turtles. No living coral grew on the peat reefs. Instead, seagrass and seaweeds grew directly on the peat, while crevices and ledges sheltered spiny lobsters, oysters, barnacles, and juvenile fish. Young snappers and grunts, usually associated with coral reefs, likely use these spaces as refuges from predators.

Each peat reef supported 26 to 36 small fish species, with species diversity comparable to the coral reef. The two reef types shared much of their fish life, even though their communities of invertebrates attached to the seabed were entirely different. Sharks, rays, and turtles were also recorded on both reef types. Green turtles and dugongs occur in the area and could graze the seagrass patches, although that potential role remains distinct from the animals documented during the surveys.

“What was once a forest floor is now a nursery for reef fish. We were surprised by how much life these ancient peat deposits support, and how many species move between them and the coral reefs nearby. This coastline has very little natural hard seabed, mostly shifting sand. When rising seas expose these old peat layers, they create rare, solid habitat where marine life can settle, hide and feed,” said Dr. Mario Lebrato, lead author and co-founder of the BCSS Ocean Observatory.

The research was enabled by the observatory’s monitoring capabilities, described in two earlier papers in Frontiers in Marine Science . Established in Mozambique’s Bazaruto Archipelago in 2017, BCSS is Africa’s first permanent Ocean Observatory. It has generated more than 22 million measurements across over 30 chemical, environmental, and biodiversity variables.

Its network spans six interconnected ecosystems and 14 long-term monitoring stations across approximately 6,850 square kilometers, or 2,645 square miles, of the greater Bazaruto seascape. The habitats monitored range from mangroves and seagrass meadows to peat and coral reefs, lagoons, seamounts, and the open ocean.

The peat reefs occupy a particularly changeable part of that seascape. Sitting just 2–4 meters deep, or about 7–13 feet, they are regularly exposed by the tides and receive much more sunlight than the deeper coral reef. Temperatures can shift between 24. 5 and 28. 6°C, or 76. 1 and 83. 5°F, within a day. Storms and cyclones bury, uncover, and break apart the peat, and many reefs disappear through erosion and sand movement as sea levels continue to rise.

“The existence of tropical peat reefs underscores the resilience and adaptive reinvention potential of coastal ecosystems under pressure from sea-level rise and shoreline change. Their contribution to biodiversity, fisheries habitat, and potential legacy-carbon preservation should be recognized in coastal management and conservation strategies, particularly in regions where coral reef health is declining. The ability to demonstrate the vitality of these habitats as a result of our continuous observation excites me for the prospect of implementing conservation policy that protects similar regions around the world,” Lebrato said.

articles.title: Indian Gen Z ‘cockroach’ protesters aim to upend assumptions about democracy – and populism – in Modi’s India
articles.dek: Five months after its founding , India’s Cockroach Janta Party, known as the CJP, has revealed what youth-led democratic movements can achieve – and how hard they are to sustain.
paragraphs: Five months after its founding , India’s Cockroach Janta Party, known as the CJP, has revealed what youth-led democratic movements can achieve – and how hard they are to sustain.

The movement was formed in May 2026 to protest the government’s cancellation of medical school entrance exams and after India’s Chief Justice Surya Kant likened unemployed youth to cockroaches. By July, the largely Gen Z movement had scored an early victory with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The CJP has since moved on to a much larger political issue: critics’ claims that the Election Commission has deleted approximately 130 million names from the voter rolls. Since Oct. 2, protesters have descended on the streets of Delhi, Mumbai and other cities demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, halting the deletions pending an independent inquiry, and the restoration of the old electoral rolls before the next elections.

In the process, the CJP has encountered strong government resistance. Amid a crackdown on protests, two of the movement’s spokespersons – Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das – were detained , while Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his right-wing populist Bharatiya Janata Party have refused to bend on the voter roll issue – instead accusing protesters of undermining democracy.

Nonetheless, as a long-time scholar of Indian political parties and social movements , I believe the CJP’s protests have revealed people’s deep-seated anxieties over democratic erosion in a country of nearly 1. 5 billion. Through courage and acerbic wit, the CJP has done something that has eluded conventional opposition parties over the past 12 years: puncturing the ruling party’s aura of invulnerability . In doing so, I believe the protests have challenged the government’s view of who “the people” are, what democracy means, and who speaks for youth, women and the politically marginalized.

Modi often describes India as the “Mother of Democracy,” a reference to its civilizational heritage and to Bharat Mata, the Hindu mother goddess. Democracy, he insists, is not a Western import but a native inheritance. The implication is meant to be reassuring: Modern India has always been democratic and always will be.

But some outside monitors disagree. Sweden’s V-Dem Institute classifies India as an “ electoral autocracy ,” meaning that although it regularly holds multiparty elections, it fails basic democratic benchmarks such as legislative and judicial checks and balances and citizens’ active political participation.
Judged by how the country treats dissent, the record is damning: using anti-terrorism laws to jail activists without trial , barricading protest sites, internet blackouts and police brutality .

By contrast, the CJP considers peaceful protest, along with upholding the country’s constitution, essential elements of democracy. Demonstrators regularly circulate images of B. R. Ambedkar – the chief architect of the Indian constitution – on posters, in slogans and in songs. Like Ambedkar, 30-year-old CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke is a Dalit, or untouchable within the Hindu caste system.

Critics argue that the Bharatiya Janata Party defines the nation through Hindu civilizational identity , which is exclusionary because it rejects India’s rich Muslim historical traditions and casts doubt on the political loyalties of the country’s Muslims, who constitute about 14% of the population – 197 million people. By contrast, the CJP draws no line between insider and outsider by faith, caste or birth, and it defines community by shared commitments.

The voter roll struggle shows what is at stake in the question. The Election Commission says the revision will remove duplicate entries, deceased voters and noncitizens . But critics worry that the burden of proof falls on voters. Consider how hard it is for poor Muslims, Dalits and migrant workers to produce decades-old birth, education and land certificates. Moreover, those whose names are struck from the electoral rolls fear being branded illegal immigrants .
While the Bharatiya Janata Party had held the prime minister’s office before, Modi’s 2014 election marked a sea change in Indian politics, disrupting the Congress Party’s dominance.

The BJP owed it electoral success in part to attracting young and first-time voters with promises of employment, economic growth and what is known in Hindi as “ achhe din aane waale hain ,” or “good days are coming.” Since the BJP took office in 2014, the country has charted strong GDP growth, but the macroeconomic success has been belied by ongoing and rampant inequality that falls especially hard on the poor and young.

The BJP claims to have fulfilled some of its more targeted campaign promises, such as engaging in merit-based public sector hiring . Yet 40% of Indian college graduates under 25 are unemployed . Paradoxically, the unemployment rate for youth who cannot read and write hovers around just 3. 4%. For college graduates, who are the Cockroach Janta Party’s main constituency, it is nearly nine times higher at roughly 29% .

Seizing on this building discontent, the CJP uses the slogan “Achhe Din” ironically, on posters and memes. Its manifesto opens: “If you are going to call us cockroaches, the least you can do is pay our rent.” It calls for making “lazy” – a code word for the unemployed – a protected political identity.

Underlying the joke is a serious point: that stigmatization of the jobless offends millions of impoverished people, something critics note is protected in the dignity and equality guarantees of articles 21 and 14 of the Constitution.

The Bharatiya Janata Party has gained women’s electoral support through a combination of targeted welfare schemes, support for increased women’s representation in legislatures and endless talk of women’s empowerment, or “nari shakti .”
However, masses of women protesters have challenged state-defined women’s empowerment. They stop police vans carrying detainees, scale barricades and criticize the prime minister.

One of the most prominent among them is Neha Bora, a Ph. D. student and president of the left-wing All India Students’ Association, whose blunt messages to Modi has seen her profile skyrocket. Modi has said he has been subject to vulgar abuses by the protesters and was shocked by how “our daughters” could use such foul language, but he viewed them as “misdirected children” and was ready to forgive them .

The throngs of women who are protesting express deep discontent with the government’s paternalism. They challenge its Hindu-inflected understanding of empowerment and insist on speaking for themselves rather than being spoken for. They express outrage at the government’s brutal response to their peaceful protests. They describe how the police have beaten and sexually harassed them, while anonymous self-styled guardians of religious morality engage in doxing, threats of rape and acid attacks, and circulate demeaning AI-generated images of them. For protesters, that record sits uneasily besides the prime minister’s denunciation of violence against women .

The CJP motto, “Cockroaches never die,” has wide resonance. Protesters have survived, but not escaped, violence, incarceration, internet blackouts and police blockades. The sunglass-wearing cockroach mascot makes a mockery of leader-centered nationalist branding.

Recent youth-led uprisings in Bangladesh and Nepal have shown how quickly online mobilization can outrun official control. What distinguishes the CJP is that it pairs humor with legal and technical infrastructure. Its online portal Saakshi vault , which means “witness,” collects photos and videos of police violence that protesters upload; volunteer lawyers use these to issue complaints against officers.

The CJP’s recent and remarkable successes do not mean that the movement is likely to disrupt the BJP’s hold on power in the next parliamentary elections in 2029. For now at least, the CJP is fairly concentrated in urban strongholds and would need to build organizational infrastructure and develop long-term demands.

However, a generation that a government minister wrote off as lazy and expendable has exposed the cracks in the system that the chief justice defended. Whatever form it takes, the movement provides a vision and reminder of what democracy looks like.

articles.title: Scientists Discover “D-Rex,” a Giant Fungus Unlike Anything Seen Before
articles.dek: A newly discovered giant fungus belongs to a previously unknown family that may have emerged around 65 million years ago, shortly after the mass extinction that killed the…
paragraphs: A newly discovered giant fungus belongs to a previously unknown family that may have emerged around 65 million years ago, shortly after the mass extinction that killed the non-avian dinosaurs.

A fungus discovered in China’s Yunnan forests produces whitish, spore-bearing structures up to 50 centimeters (about 20 inches) tall and weighing as much as 2. 2 kilograms (4. 9 pounds). The newly described species, Dianjunus rex , has the largest known fruiting bodies in the fungal phylum Ascomycota, surpassing previous record holders that stood 20 to 30 centimeters (about 8 to 12 inches) tall.

Ascomycota is the largest group of fungi, with more than 64,000 species. Its members, called ascomycetes, do not grow true mushrooms. Instead, they release spores from tiny, sac-like structures inside or on the surfaces of their fruiting bodies. For D. rex , producing such large reproductive structures could offer an advantage in a crowded forest, although the researchers have not established why it grows so big.

“A fruiting body which towers above surrounding vegetation and debris could have better dispersal of spores by wind in dense forests. However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs,” hypothesized Dr. Indunil C Senanayake, the study’s corresponding author and an associate professor at the Germplasm Bank of Wild Species of the Kunming Institute of Botany in China.

Scientists from the institute encountered the fungus during fieldwork in temperate coniferous forests near Damaidi and Yipinglang and in tropical rainforest near Nanbang. Its upright fruiting bodies, known as stromata, grew on the woody roots of Chinese cork oak, emerging from the rhizosphere, the soil immediately surrounding the roots. Senanayake said, “The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests.”

To investigate what they had found, the researchers collected fruiting bodies and deposited voucher specimens in the Kunming Institute of Botany’s collections. They grew spores on laboratory media to study the fungus’s form and structure and sequenced its genome, including its full set of protein-coding genes.

The genetic results, supported by the detailed examination of its morphology, established a new species and genus within the order Xylariales. The findings, published in Frontiers in Fungal Biology , also warranted recognition at a broader level of classification.
“This remarkable species represents a new fungal family, Dianjunaceae, and provides a rare window into the evolution of extreme fungal body forms,” said Senanayake.

The researchers chose the name Dianjunus rex for the fungus’s regal size and the ancient Dian kingdom. Its closest known relative, Graphostroma platystoma , grows on dead hardwood across the Northern Hemisphere and is itself the sole member of another family, Graphostromataceae.

Other fungi in Xylariales are known for producing secondary compounds, chemicals beyond those essential for basic growth, as well as enzymes that break down complex plant molecules. Similar enzymes might help “D-rex” digest dead wood, a possibility that gives context to the researchers’ investigation of its evolutionary origins.

Using a molecular clock analysis, which estimates evolutionary timing from genetic differences, the team compared the new species’ DNA with genomes from hundreds of fungi with known evolutionary ages. The results suggested that the Dianjunaceae family arose around 65 million years ago, roughly one million years after the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction. That event wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs and countless other animals and plants.

“This timing raises an intriguing possibility. After the mass extinction, forests experienced dramatic changes, including the sudden availability of large amounts of dead plant material,” said Senanayake. “For wood-associated decomposing fungi, such environmental disruption may have created new ecological opportunities.”
The researchers expect more fungal discoveries in subtropical China, where conditions favor diversification but finding and documenting species remains difficult.

“This region combines exceptional habitat heterogeneity, climatic stability, and complex biotic interactions that promote fungal diversification. Historically, however, fungal diversity in these ecosystems has been underestimated due to logistical difficulties in field sampling, the seasonal and cryptic nature of fungal fruiting, and a historical emphasis on economically important fungi,” said Senanayake.

paragraphs: New Guinea, the world’s second-largest island, harbors an extraordinary variety of plant life across more than a dozen distinct ecoregions , including seasonally dry savannas, tropical rainforests, and lowland swamp forests. But in September and October 2026, as drought gripped New Guinea (sometimes called Papua) amid a strong El Niño , fires scorched the island and smoke shrouded large swaths of it for weeks.

The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite captured this image of thick smoke streaming from the southern part of the island on October 11, 2026. In recent weeks, soaring levels of air pollution delayed and canceled flights , closed schools, and prompted officials in some areas to urge children and older people to wear masks.

“Sometimes smoke that has drifted into the convection of nearby thunderstorms will get washed out or lofted up into the upper troposphere, but a lot of smoke stays near the surface and causes air quality problems,” said Robert Field, an associate research scientist at NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies and Columbia University. “It’s a horrible situation.”

According to the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), a fire emissions monitoring system, fires in Papua New Guinea, on the eastern half of the island, had released nearly 32 megatons of carbon by October 17, more than any other year on record at that point in the year (charts above). “Emissions are already much higher than the 2015 total for the year, and it’s very likely that this will become the highest year on record for Papua New Guinea, even surpassing 1997,” said Guido van der Werf, a fire scientist at Wageningen University & Research.

On the Indonesian side, sometimes called West New Guinea or Indonesian Papua, carbon emissions exceeded 35 megatons , the third highest after 2015 and 1997, other El Niño years with severe fires. Van der Werf led the development of GFED, a satellite-driven modeling framework that uses a mix of remote sensing , vegetation characteristics, and other information to estimate the extent of vegetation fires and the emissions over nearly three decades.

Unusually dry weather—a byproduct of El Niño shifting rainfall patterns —has primed ecosystems across the island to burn. The southernmost part of Papua New Guinea, dominated by relatively fire-prone savannas and grasslands of the Trans-Fly region , went more than 90 consecutive days without rain, according to Papua New Guinea’s National Weather Service . Since August, parts of the region have seen precipitation of roughly 5 to 10 percent of normal, according to the weather service’s data. Local news outlets report that drought is causing crop failures , water shortages , and school disruptions .

In this normally wet part of the world, people ignite the vast majority of fires, researchers say. Crop fires, pasture maintenance, deforestation and land clearing, and hunting are all common reasons people burn in New Guinea. In dry conditions, managed fires sometimes spread and burn uncontrolled as wildfires, particularly in the drier, southernmost parts of the island.

“We’re seeing an exceptionally high level of fire activity in Papua New Guinea and Eastern Indonesia, particularly Indonesian Papua and Kalimantan, this year compared with Sumatra and other parts of Western Indonesia,” said Yang Chen, an associate researcher at the University of California, Irvine. “Papua has emerged as Indonesia’s new deforestation frontier.”

Over the past two decades , land in Indonesian Papua has been cleared for industrial oil palm and pulpwood plantations, shifting small-scale cultivation, urban expansion, and mining . According to Global Forest Watch, the region lost 27,000 hectares of primary forest in 2025, nearly double the 2024 total and the most since 2017.

Sumatra’s fires are relatively low compared to other drought years partly because many areas are already developed. “Areas with large oil palm, sugarcane, or pulpwood plantations also often have their own private fire brigades to protect their assets,” said Field. “It’s in unmanaged areas or primary forest edges where we’re generally seeing the most fire.”
Researchers expect the fires to continue until the heavy rains of the wet season arrive in the southern part of New Guinea, typically in early November.
